topic: Dimensional Leap: The Geometry of Non-Square Matrices
target_audience: Undergraduate students in Linear Algebra or Computer Science

sections.title: The Bridge Between Worlds: Introduction
sections.content: Establish the fundamental shift from square matrices (which transform space within the same dimension) to non-square matrices (which move vectors between dimensions). Introduce the 'Landing Pad' rule: the columns of a matrix tell us where the basis vectors of the input space land in the output space.
sections.example: Visualizing a 2x2 matrix as a transformation of a square grid on a rubber sheet, then contrasting it with a 3x2 matrix that 'lifts' that sheet into a 3D room.

sections.title: Prerequisite Check: The DNA of a Matrix
sections.content: Briefly review basis vectors (i-hat and j-hat). Explain that the number of columns represents the number of input basis vectors (input dimension), and the number of rows represents the coordinates needed to describe their new positions (output dimension).
sections.example: Showing a vector [x, y] and highlighting how the matrix columns act as instructions for 'how much' of each new basis vector to use.

sections.title: Tall Matrices: Upgrading Dimensions (2D to 3D)
sections.content: Explore 'Tall' matrices (m > n, e.g., 3x2). Geometrically, this maps a lower-dimensional space into a higher-dimensional one. The 2D input space is transformed into a 'thin' 2D plane slicing through 3D space. There is no 'volume' in the output, only a flat surface embedded in a 3D world.
sections.example: A 2D 'Paper Mario' character being projected onto a slanted 2D billboard inside a 3D city. The character remains flat, but their coordinates are now (x, y, z).

sections.title: Wide Matrices: The Great Squashing (3D to 2D)
sections.content: Explore 'Wide' matrices (m < n, e.g., 2x3). This maps a higher-dimensional space into a lower-dimensional one. This process involves a 'projection' or 'collapsing' where information is inevitably lost (the Null Space). Space is compressed.
sections.example: A 3D bird flying in the sky. A 2x3 matrix acts like a sun directly overhead, projecting the bird's 3D movement onto its 2D shadow on the ground. The height (z-axis) info is squashed to zero.

sections.title: Summary & The 'Grid' Intuition
sections.content: Consolidate the rule: Rows = Output Dimension, Columns = Input Dimension. Reinforce that non-square matrices represent transformations that either 'embed' or 'project'. Visual summary showing the 'Tall' matrix expanding coordinates and the 'Wide' matrix reducing them.
sections.example: A summary animation: A 2D grid stretching into a 3D plane (Tall), followed by a 3D cube being flattened into a 2D square (Wide), labeled with their respective matrix dimensions.
